1.title: AI-Specific Laws: the EU AI Act and Beyond
1.text: Welcome to Module six: A I-Specific Laws. This is the largest module, because competency C of domain two is the heaviest part of the legal domain. We start with the E U A I Act in depth: scope, risk classes, requirements, roles, enforcement and timeline. Then we compare South Korea, the United States and other approaches.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Place a system in the right risk class, and say what each class means. List the requirements for high-risk systems and the duties that come with them. Explain human oversight, transparency and quality management. Explain the extra rules for general-purpose A I models. Explain enforcement, penalties and duties by role. And compare the South Korean, U S and other approaches.

1.title: Case Check-In: Which Helios System Is Regulated, and How?
1.text: At Helios, the hiring tool screens applicants in the E U, and Veridex also offers emotion analysis of the video interview. The customer assistant chats with E U customers, on a general-purpose model from Corvid Labs. Helios also hires in New York City, Illinois and Colorado, and serves customers in South Korea. Jonas Weber asks: which class, which duties, which role, and what is the penalty if we get it wrong?

1.title: The EU AI Act at a Glance: Reach and Scope
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The A I Act is a risk-based law: the higher the risk, the heavier the duty. Under Article two, it applies to providers that place systems or general-purpose models on the E U market, wherever they are based. It applies to deployers in the E U, and to third-country providers and deployers when the output is used in the E U. It also covers importers, distributors, product manufacturers, authorized representatives and affected persons. Excluded are military, defense and national security, research before market placement, personal non-professional use, and certain open-source systems. Exam tip: use in the E U matters, not location.

1.title: Key Definitions That Decide Scope
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Article three holds the definitions that decide scope. An A I system infers outputs from input, as we saw in module one. The provider develops and places on the market; the deployer uses under its authority. Placing on the market is the first making available on the Union market. Putting into service is supply for first use to the deployer, or for own use. A general-purpose model shows significant generality. The intended purpose drives classification, and a substantial modification can change duties and roles. Exam tip: classification follows the use, not the technology.

1.title: The Four Risk Classes
1.text: The Act has four risk classes. Unacceptable risk: practices that are banned, in Article five. High risk: allowed, but under strict requirements, through two routes, Annex one for product safety and Annex three for listed uses. Limited risk: transparency duties, such as telling people they talk to A I, in Article fifty. Minimal risk: no specific duties. General-purpose A I models have their own track of obligations. Exam tip: name the class first. The duties follow from it.

1.title: Prohibited Practices
1.text: This slide is tagged dates. Article five bans these practices. Manipulation through subliminal or deceptive techniques causing significant harm. Exploiting vulnerabilities of age, disability or social or economic situation. Social scoring. Crime prediction based solely on profiling. Building face databases by untargeted scraping. Inferring emotions in the workplace and in education, except for medical or safety reasons. Biometric categorization of sensitive traits. And real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement, unless strictly necessary. The new bans on non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material apply from the second of December, twenty twenty-six. The older bans apply since the second of February, twenty twenty-five.

1.title: High-Risk, Route One: Product Safety (Annex I)
1.text: Route one to high risk is product safety. Under Article six, paragraph one, a system is high-risk when it is a safety component of a product, or a product itself, covered by Annex one harmonized legislation, and that product needs a third-party conformity assessment. Typical examples are machinery, medical devices, vehicles and toys. Route two, in Article six, paragraph two, is a use listed in Annex three. Both routes lead to the same requirements, with different assessment procedures. Exam tip: a medical-device component and a hiring tool are both high-risk, through different doors.

1.title: High-Risk, Route Two: The Annex III Areas
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Annex three lists eight areas. Biometrics, including remote identification, categorization and emotion recognition. Critical infrastructure safety components. Education: admission, assessing learning and monitoring tests. Employment: recruitment and selection, and decisions on promotion, termination, task allocation and monitoring. Essential services: public benefits, credit scoring, life and health insurance pricing, and emergency triage. Law enforcement. Migration, asylum and border control. And justice and democratic processes. Exam tip: hiring and credit scoring are high-risk by listing. Fraud detection is carved out of credit.

1.title: Is It High-Risk? The Article 6(3) Filter
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Walk four steps. One: is the practice prohibited? Then stop. Two: is it a safety component of an Annex one product? Then high-risk. Three: is the use listed in Annex three? Then high-risk. Four, the filter in Article six, paragraph three. A listed system is not high-risk only if it poses no significant risk of harm and fits one of four cases: a narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting patterns without replacing human assessment, or a preparatory task. But a system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk. A provider that decides otherwise must document and register that assessment.

1.title: Limited and Minimal Risk, and General-Purpose Models
1.text: Limited risk covers systems that interact with people, generate synthetic content, or infer emotions: they carry transparency duties under Article fifty. Minimal risk is most A I, such as spam filters, with no specific duties beyond voluntary codes. General-purpose models are a separate track, with obligations on the model provider. A general-purpose model placed in a high-risk use makes the system high-risk, and the system's provider carries those duties. Exam tip: a chatbot is limited risk for transparency, and becomes high-risk only if its use is on a high-risk list.

1.title: Applying the Classes to Helios
1.text: Now apply the classes to Helios. The hiring tool is high-risk: Annex three employment covers recruitment and selection, and it profiles people, so there is no Article six paragraph three escape. The emotion analysis of the video interview is prohibited in the E U workplace, unless used for medical or safety reasons. The customer assistant is limited risk: customers must be told it is A I. The Corvid Labs model underneath is a general-purpose model, whose provider has its own duties. Helios switches off emotion analysis in the E U, and prepares for high-risk duties. Exam tip: walk the path in order.

2.title: The High-Risk Requirements at a Glance
2.text: High-risk systems must meet seven requirements, in Articles nine to fifteen. Article nine: a risk management system. Article ten: data and data governance. Article eleven: technical documentation. Article twelve: record-keeping, or logs. Article thirteen: transparency and instructions for use. Article fourteen: human oversight. Article fifteen: accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. The provider must meet them, and the deployer relies on and supports them. Exam tip: learn the seven by their job: manage risk, govern data, document, log, tell, oversee, secure.

2.title: Risk Management System (Article 9)
2.text: Article nine requires a risk management system. It is a continuous, iterative process, planned and run through the whole life cycle. Identify and analyze known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights. Estimate and evaluate them, including from foreseeable misuse and post-market data. Adopt targeted measures and judge residual risk acceptable: design it out first, then mitigate, then inform and train. Test against predefined metrics before market placement. And consider persons under eighteen and other vulnerable groups. Exam tip: it is a living process, not a one-time assessment.

2.title: Data and Data Governance (Article 10)
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged verify live. Data governance under Article ten covers design choices, data origin and collection, preparation such as annotation and cleaning, assumptions, and availability and suitability. Providers must examine possible biases that could harm health, safety or fundamental rights, or lead to prohibited discrimination, and take measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them. Datasets should be relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors as far as possible, and complete. The Digital Omnibus added Article four A: special-category data may be processed exceptionally for bias detection and correction, only where strictly necessary and under strict conditions. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, this rule is new.

2.title: Technical Documentation and Record-Keeping (Articles 11 and 12)
2.text: Technical documentation is drawn up before placing on the market, kept up to date, and shows compliance. It has the minimum elements of Annex four. Small and medium enterprises may use a simplified form. A post-market monitoring plan is part of that documentation. Under Article twelve, the system must automatically record events over its lifetime, to identify risk situations, to support post-market monitoring, and to let deployers monitor operation. Remote biometric identification logs add the time of use, the database checked, the matched input, and who verified. Exam tip: documentation is for assessors. Logs trace what the system did.

2.title: Transparency to Deployers and Accuracy, Robustness, Cybersecurity (Articles 13 and 15)
2.text: Article thirteen requires instructions for use stating the provider's identity, the system's capabilities and limits, pre-determined changes, human oversight measures, resources and lifetime, and log collection. Article fifteen then sets accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Accuracy levels and metrics are declared in the instructions. Robustness means resilience to errors, faults and inconsistencies, and reducing feedback loops where the system keeps learning. Cybersecurity means resisting attempts to alter use or output, including data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples and confidentiality attacks. Exam tip: transparency here is information for the deployer. Notices to the public sit in Article fifty.

2.title: Conformity Assessment, Declaration, CE Marking and Registration
2.text: Before a high-risk system goes to market, the provider completes conformity assessment under Article forty-three. For most Annex three uses, that is internal control by the provider. For biometrics, it is internal control or a notified body, depending on standards. Annex one products follow the sectoral procedure. The provider draws up the E U declaration of conformity under Article forty-seven, affixes the C E marking under Article forty-eight, and registers the system under Article forty-nine. A substantial modification needs a new assessment, but changes pre-determined for a learning system are not substantial. Exam tip: mostly self-assessment.

2.title: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27)
2.text: Article twenty-seven requires a fundamental rights impact assessment from certain deployers. Who: public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of credit-scoring and life and health insurance systems, but not for critical infrastructure systems. When: before first use, updated if elements change. Content: the process, the period and frequency of use, the groups affected, the specific risks of harm, human oversight, and measures if risks materialize, including complaint mechanisms. The deployer notifies the market surveillance authority, and may cross-refer to a G D P R data protection impact assessment. Exam tip: it complements the provider's risk management.

2.title: Post-Market Monitoring and Serious Incident Reporting (Articles 72 and 73)
2.text: Under Article seventy-two, providers run a post-market monitoring system, proportionate to the technology and risks, that collects and analyzes performance data over the system's lifetime. The plan belongs to the technical documentation. Under Article seventy-three, a serious incident is reported immediately after a causal link is established, and in any event not later than fifteen days after awareness. For a widespread infringement or the most serious disruptions, the limit is two days. After a death, it is ten days. Deployers tell the provider and authorities when they suspect a risk or a serious incident. Exam tip: two days, ten days, fifteen days.

2.title: Human Oversight (Article 14)
2.text: Human oversight under Article fourteen aims to prevent or minimize risks to health, safety and fundamental rights, including from foreseeable misuse. Overseers must be able to understand the system's capacities and limits; stay aware of automation bias; interpret output correctly; override or disregard output, or decide not to use the system; and stop it. For remote biometric identification, a result is acted on only after separate verification by two people. The provider designs the measures in, and the deployer assigns competent, trained people with authority. Exam tip: oversight must be effective, not nominal.

2.title: Transparency and Notification Duties (Article 50)
2.text: Article fifty sets four transparency duties. When a system interacts directly with people, the provider designs it so people know they are dealing with A I, unless it is obvious. When a system generates synthetic audio, image, video or text, the provider marks outputs in a machine-readable format. For emotion recognition or biometric categorization, the deployer informs the exposed people. For deepfakes and A I text published to inform the public, the deployer discloses that it is artificial, with editorial-control exceptions. Information is given clearly, at the latest at first interaction. Exam tip: telling customers they chat with A I is the provider's design duty.

2.title: Quality Management System (Article 17)
2.text: Article seventeen requires a quality management system: a documented system of policies, procedures and instructions that keeps the provider compliant. It covers a compliance strategy, design and development controls, testing and validation, technical specifications, data management, risk management, post-market monitoring, serious incident reporting, communication with authorities, record-keeping, resource management and accountability. It is applied proportionately to the provider's size, with consideration for small and medium enterprises. Exam tip: the quality system ties the requirements together. It does not replace any of them.

2.title: General-Purpose AI Models: Obligations of All Providers
2.text: This slide is tagged dates. Every provider of a general-purpose model has four duties under Article fifty-three. Keep technical documentation of the model, including training and testing, under Annex eleven. Provide information and documentation for downstream providers who build the model into systems, under Annex twelve, while protecting intellectual property and trade secrets. Put in place a copyright policy that honors rights reservations. And publish a summary of training content, using the A I Office template. These rules apply from the second of August, twenty twenty-five. Exam tip: these four apply to every model.

2.title: Models With Systemic Risk (Articles 51 and 55)
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. A model has systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities. That is presumed when training used more than ten to the power of twenty-five floating point operations, or when the Commission so decides, under Article fifty-one. Article fifty-five adds duties: evaluate the model, including adversarial testing; assess and mitigate systemic risks at E U level; track and report serious incidents to the A I Office; and ensure cybersecurity. At Helios, Corvid Labs carries these model-level duties, and Helios asks for the model documentation. Exam tip: the compute threshold gives a presumption.

2.title: Codes of Practice, Open Source and the Provider Chain
2.text: This slide is tagged dates. The A I Office encourages codes of practice for the model duties, which were due by the second of May, twenty twenty-five. If a code is not finalized by the second of August, twenty twenty-five, or is inadequate, the Commission may set common rules by implementing act. Providers can show compliance through a code, harmonized standards, or other adequate means. Free and open-source models get relief from some duties, but not from the copyright policy and training summary, and not if they carry systemic risk. Downstream providers rely on the model provider's information. Exam tip: a code is a route to show compliance.

2.title: Governance and Who Enforces
2.text: At European level, the A I Office, inside the Commission, oversees general-purpose models, and the A I Board helps coordinate. At national level, each Member State designates at least one market surveillance authority and one notifying authority, acting independently. Notified bodies perform third-party conformity assessment where required. Market surveillance authorities can require corrective action, withdraw or recall systems, and impose fines. The European Data Protection Supervisor supervises E U institutions. Exam tip: general-purpose model enforcement is European. Most system enforcement is national.

2.title: Penalties
2.text: The Act has three fine tiers. For prohibited practices under Article five: up to thirty-five million euros or seven percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. For most other obligations, covering providers, importers, distributors, deployers, authorized representatives, notified bodies and transparency: up to fifteen million euros or three percent. For incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities: up to seven and a half million euros or one percent. For small and medium enterprises and start-ups, the lower applies. General-purpose model providers face up to three percent or fifteen million euros, from the Commission. Exam tip: do not confuse the G D P R's twenty million and four percent.

2.title: The Timeline
2.text: This slide is tagged dates and verify live. On the second of February, twenty twenty-five, the prohibitions and the A I literacy duty began to apply. On the second of August, twenty twenty-five, the general-purpose model rules, the governance provisions and most penalties provisions followed. On the second of August, twenty twenty-six, the Act applies generally, including transparency duties. On the second of December, twenty twenty-six, the new bans on sexual imagery apply. The Annex three high-risk rules now apply from the second of December, twenty twenty-seven, and the Annex one rules from the second of August, twenty twenty-eight, as amended. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, check for further changes.

3.title: Duties by Role: Providers, Importers, Distributors, Authorized Representatives
3.text: Now duties by role. The provider, under Article sixteen, meets the requirements, runs a quality management system, keeps documentation and logs, completes conformity assessment, draws up the declaration, affixes the C E marking, registers the system, and takes corrective action. The importer, under Article twenty-three, verifies conformity, documentation, marking and instructions before placing on the market, and keeps key documents for ten years. The distributor checks marking, documentation and instructions, and stops if non-conforming. The authorized representative acts for a non-E U provider under a written mandate. Exam tip: importers and distributors verify before they supply.

3.title: Deployer Duties and When a Role Changes
3.text: Deployers have their own duties under Article twenty-six. Use the system per its instructions, and assign human oversight to people with competence, training and authority. Ensure input data under your control are relevant and sufficiently representative. Monitor, tell the provider, suspend use where there is a risk, and report serious incidents, the provider first and then the authorities. Keep logs for at least six months. Inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use, and inform people subject to decisions. And under Article twenty-five, a deployer becomes a provider if it puts its name on a high-risk system, makes a substantial modification, or changes the intended purpose so it becomes high-risk. Exam tip: rebranding or repurposing moves provider duties onto you.

3.title: South Korea: The AI Basic Act
3.text: This slide is tagged verify live, because these details rest on secondary sources. South Korea's A I Basic Act has been in force since the twenty-second of January, twenty twenty-six. It focuses on high-impact A I, in areas such as healthcare, hiring and lending, with duties for risk management, user notice and human oversight. For generative A I, it requires advance notice to users and labeling of generated output. Foreign operators above set thresholds appoint a domestic representative. Fines reach thirty million won, and a grace period of at least a year was announced. Exam tip: Korea resembles the E U in risk focus, with lighter penalties.

3.title: The US Federal Position
3.text: This slide is tagged verify live. The United States has no comprehensive federal A I statute. Agencies apply existing laws: the F T C on deception and unfairness, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission on employment, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau on credit, and others. Federal policy has moved toward removing barriers and uniform national rules. Executive Order fourteen thousand three hundred sixty-five, of the eleventh of December, twenty twenty-five, directed a federal challenge to state A I laws, and a Justice Department task force was formalized on the ninth of January, twenty twenty-six. On the twentieth of March, twenty twenty-six, the White House released non-binding recommendations to preempt state laws. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, no federal statute preempts them.

3.title: US State and Local AI Laws
3.text: This slide is tagged verify live. Colorado's twenty twenty-four A I Act was delayed to the thirtieth of June, twenty twenty-six, then repealed and replaced by Senate Bill twenty-six dash one eighty-nine, signed on the fourteenth of May. It takes effect on the first of January, twenty twenty-seven: consumer notice, explanations of adverse decisions and human review. Texas has a narrow ban on intentionally harmful uses, with Attorney General enforcement and a sandbox. California has frontier-model transparency and incident reporting, effective the first of January, twenty twenty-six, plus privacy rules on automated decision-making. Illinois requires notice of A I in employment decisions. New York City requires an annual independent bias audit and candidate notice for hiring tools.

3.title: Other Jurisdictions: Approaches Compared
3.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged verify live. The Study Guide says the credential covers other jurisdictions, so know the approaches. Risk-based statutes: the E U A I Act, South Korea, and Brazil's bill. Principles-based, regulator-led: the U K, with no general A I statute, and Japan's promotion-oriented law, leaning on cooperation and existing law. Technology-specific rules: China regulates algorithms, generative A I services and the labeling of A I-generated content. International instruments: the Council of Europe Framework Convention on A I, the first binding A I treaty, opened on the fifth of September, twenty twenty-four, and the O E C D principles. Exam tip: expect approaches, not article numbers.

3.title: Which Instrument Applies? A Decision Aid
3.text: Here is a decision aid. First, where is the system used, and who is affected? That selects the jurisdictions. Second, what does it do? That gives the class and the requirements. Third, who are you in the chain? That gives your duties. Fourth, which existing laws also apply, such as privacy, nondiscrimination, consumer protection, I P and liability, and which framework organizes the work, which is module seven. For Helios: the E U A I Act for the hiring tool and assistant, New York City and Illinois rules, the G D P R, nondiscrimination law, and Korea for its Korean customers. Exam tip: A I-specific laws sit on top of existing laws.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap. The classes: prohibited, high-risk through Annex one and Annex three, transparency, and minimal, with general-purpose models on their own track. High-risk means the Article nine to fifteen requirements, conformity assessment, registration, the rights assessment, post-market monitoring, and incident reports at fifteen, ten and two days. Oversight must be effective, people must be told they deal with A I, and a quality system ties it together. General-purpose models have four duties for all and more for systemic risk. Fines reach thirty-five million euros or seven percent, fifteen million or three, and seven and a half million or one. And roles carry different duties.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. Helios's hiring tool screens and ranks job applicants in the E U. How does the A I Act classify it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Employment, including recruitment and selection, is an Annex three area, and a system that profiles people cannot use the Article six, paragraph three exception. Recruitment A I is not banned, and a human decision does not make it minimal.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. Which two practices are prohibited under Article five of the A I Act? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Workplace emotion inference, except for medical or safety reasons, and untargeted facial scraping are banned. A spam filter is minimal risk, credit scoring is a high-risk use, and a chatbot notice is a transparency duty that the Act requires.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. A provider of a high-risk system must run a continuous, iterative process throughout the system's life cycle to identify and reduce foreseeable risks. Which requirement is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Article nine requires a risk management system that is a continuous iterative process, planned and run throughout the entire life cycle.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. Helios's customer assistant chats directly with E U customers and is not used for any high-risk purpose. Which duty most directly applies? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A system that interacts directly with people carries a transparency duty under Article fifty: people must be told they are dealing with A I, unless it is obvious. The other options belong to high-risk systems.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. Corvid Labs trains a general-purpose model using more than ten to the power of twenty-five floating point operations. What follows under the A I Act? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Training above that threshold creates a presumption of systemic risk, which adds duties such as evaluation with adversarial testing, risk mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity.

3.title: Practice Question 6
3.text: Question six. What is the maximum fine for using a prohibited A I practice under the A I Act? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: thirty-five million euros or seven percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. The lower tiers cover other obligations and incorrect information, and twenty million euros and four percent belongs to the G D P R.

3.title: Practice Question 7
3.text: Question seven. Helios deploys the Veridex hiring tool, which is a high-risk system. Which two duties fall on Helios as the deployer? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Deployers use the system as instructed, assign competent oversight, and inform workers' representatives and affected people. The declaration, marking, quality system, registration and documentation are provider duties.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: B. Question two: A and D. Question three: C. Question four: D. Question five: B. Question six: C. Question seven: B and E. That completes Module six. Next, Module seven covers standards and frameworks: the O E C D principles, the N I S T A I Risk Management Framework, and the I S O standards.
